newsitem.title: FRANCE: Top French parliamentarian sentenced for slander.
newsitem.headline: Top French parliamentarian sentenced for slander.

text.p: The president of the French National Assembly's Law Commission was fined 30,000 francs ($6,000) on Tuesday for slandering a magistrate delving into suspected corruption in the ruling Gaullist party.
Gaullist Pierre Mazeaud was also ordered to pay magistrate Eric Halphen a symbolic franc (20 cents) damages plus 10,000 francs ($2,000) legal costs, the court ruled.
Halphen sued over in a newspaper interview in which Mazeaud acccused him of tipping off the press before a police search at the home of Paris mayor Jean Tiberi, a leading Gaullist.

The long-running investigation, in which several Gaullist officials have been placed under investigation, seeks to establish the scope of payments to the Paris municipality by private contractors before Tiberi succeeded President Jacques Chirac as mayor in May 1985.
The court which heard Halphen's complaint ruled that Mazeaud "based himself on erroneous information, without seeking to check its veracity, and showed no objectivity."

Mazeaud had also criticised Halphen's handling of a case in which Tiberi's son was accused of occupying a low-cost flat rented from the municipality, despite owning his own flat and having the city's flat refurbished at public expense.
The libel trial took place a day after Chirac launched a major reform of the French justice system which he said aimed at ensuring greater independence for the judiciary from the government.
